169	    How a request moves
170	## Functional core, imperative shell
171	Everything that touches the network or the database sits at the edges and stays thin. The rules (rank maths, the search pattern, applying a partial update, mapping rows to responses) are pure functions that never mutate their input, in a core that the unit tests reach directly. FastAPI's Depends composes each request from small providers. Errors are raised as domain exceptions and turned into HTTP status codes in one place.
172	          RequestJSON · cookie
173	          Middlewareid · log · errors
174	          RouterPydantic in/out
175	          Serviceone transaction
176	          Repositoryowner filter
177	          Postgresasyncpg
178	          model
179	          call
180	          SQL
181	          raises NotFound, Conflict, Invalid → 404, 409, 400 envelope
182	          Depends()session · current user
183	          injects
184	          Domain core · purerank_between · search_pattern · apply_patch
185	          calls, no I/O
186	The shaded box is the only place business rules live, and nothing in it does I/O. Every repository query filters on owner_id, so ownership is enforced in the SQL itself, not checked after a row is loaded.
187	    Many users at once · FastAPI and uvicorn
188	## Async and concurrency
189	Each API replica is one uvicorn process running one event loop. The loop can hold thousands of open requests, but only while each of them is waiting on I/O. Anything that keeps the loop busy (a slow hash, a blocking call, a synchronous write) stalls every request on that replica at once. So the design has three jobs: never block the loop, put a limit on every shared resource, and when a limit is reached, make requests queue for a bounded time or get a clear 503 rather than pile up.
190	          one API replica · one uvicorn process
191	          nginx
192	          keep-alive
193	          HTTP
194	          event loop · uvloop
195	          ≤ 200 requests at once
196	          over the limit → 503
197	          AsyncSession
198	          one per request
199	          connection pool
200	          10 + 5 · wait ≤ 5 s
201	          Semaphore(4)
202	          argon2 hashes
203	          thread pool
204	          hash runs off the loop
205	          QueueHandler
206	          never blocks
207	          listener thread
208	          JSON lines → stdout
209	          Postgres
210	          100 conns
211	          await
212	          login
213	          log
214	          borrow
215	          to_thread
216	          enqueue
217	          asyncpg
218	Everything the loop hands off has a limit: 200 requests in progress per replica, 15 database connections, 4 hashes at a time. When a limit is reached, requests wait for a bounded time; past that wait the client gets a 503 with the error envelope, never a hung connection.
219	D13
220	### One uvicorn process per container, every handler asynclocked
221	Choice
222	uvicorn[standard] (uvloop, httptools) with one worker per container; more capacity means more replicas. Every route is async def and uses only async libraries. --limit-concurrency 200 answers 503 past 200 in-flight requests. --timeout-graceful-shutdown 20 lets in-flight requests finish on SIGTERM, then the lifespan closes the pool. Nginx keeps connections to the API open and caps request bodies at 64 KB.
223	Instead of
224	Gunicorn or uvicorn managing several worker processes inside one container. Or plain def handlers, which FastAPI runs on a thread pool capped at 40 threads by default.
225	Why
226	One process per container lets Docker and Kubernetes restart it, count it and scale it, and each pod's memory and CPU stay predictable. Async-only handlers mean the loop is the only scheduler to reason about.
227	D14
228	### Password hashing runs off the loop, at most four at a timelocked
229	Choice
230	argon2id with OWASP's parameters (19 MiB memory, 2 passes, 1 lane), run through asyncio.to_thread behind an asyncio.Semaphore(4) per process. argon2-cffi releases the GIL while it hashes, so the hashes really do run in parallel with the loop.
231	Instead of
232	Hashing on the loop, or without a limit.
233	Why
234	One hash takes tens of milliseconds of CPU. On the loop, every sign-in would freeze that replica for that long. Without a limit, a burst of sign-ins would exhaust memory: the library's default profile uses 64 MiB per hash, so 100 sign-ins at once would need over 6 GB. With the semaphore, extra sign-ins wait their turn instead.
235	D15
236	### A connection budget, and timeouts on every waitlocked
237	Choice
238	Async SQLAlchemy on asyncpg. Each replica has a pool of 10 connections plus 5 overflow, a 5-second wait for a free one, and pool_pre_ping. Postgres runs with statement_timeout 5 s and idle_in_transaction_session_timeout 10 s. Each request gets its own AsyncSession and one transaction, committed on success and rolled back on any exception. Sessions are never shared between concurrent coroutines, because an AsyncSession isn't safe for that.
239	Budget
240	Total connections = replicas × 15, kept under 80% of Postgres's 100. That's 30 in round 1 and 45 in round 2. Round 3 adds autoscaling, so it puts the PgBouncer built into Azure's Postgres in front.
241	Why
242	Requests are short, so 15 connections serve many concurrent users. When load exceeds that, requests wait up to 5 seconds and then get a clear 503, rather than an unbounded queue taking down the database.
243	Reported
244	The final report states, for each round, how many concurrent users the stack served within budget, measured by D18 rather than estimated.
245	    Many requests touching the same rows
246	## Races and consistency
247	Tasks are private, so two different users never contend for the same row. The races that remain come from one user (two tabs, fast drags, a double-click) and from users signing up with the same email. Every guard lives in Postgres, because a lock inside one Python process means nothing to the other replica.
248	          api-1 · move X
249	          Postgres
250	          api-2 · move Y
251	          waits
252	          BEGIN · lock(owner) granted
253	          BEGIN · lock(owner)
254	          read neighbours a0 | a1
255	          write X = a0V · COMMIT
256	          lock granted
257	          read neighbours a0 | a0V
258	          write Y = a0F · COMMIT
259	          Final order: A a0 · Y a0F · X a0V · B a1
260	Both requests ask to place a task right after A. The shaded bars show who holds the per-user lock (pg_advisory_xact_lock on the owner id; it's released at commit). Without it, both would read a0 | a1 and both would write a0V. The unique index on (owner_id, rank) would then reject one, and the user would see an error instead of a silent tie. Other users' writes never wait for this lock.
261	D16
262	### Order changes are serialized per user, in Postgreslocked
263	Choice
264	Creating a task and moving one each start their transaction with pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtextextended(owner_id::text, 0)), then read the neighbours, compute the rank and write. A unique index on (owner_id, rank) backs it up. Edits and deletes don't take the lock, since they never change ranks.
265	Isolation
266	Postgres's default, READ COMMITTED, and that's deliberate. Each statement reads a fresh snapshot, so the neighbour read after the lock is granted sees the other move's commit. Under REPEATABLE READ the snapshot would be taken at the lock statement, before that commit, and both moves would compute the same rank.
267	Instead of
268	An asyncio.Lock, which only covers one process. SERIALIZABLE everywhere, which needs retry loops on every write. A version check on the whole list.
269	Why
270	The lock is the narrowest correct one: one user's ordering writes queue for a few milliseconds, and nothing else waits.
271	Testing
272	The race tests run with the lead present. We watch them fail with the lock removed, then pass with it in place, before the backend PR is raised.
273	D17
274	### Tabs stay fresh, and edits can't silently overwrite each otherlocked
275	The case
276	Tab 2 loaded a task before tab 1 saved a change to it. Tab 2 then saves its stale copy, and tab 1's change is silently lost.
277	Choice
278	Two layers. First, freshness: whenever a tab regains focus or the network comes back, TanStack Query refetches what's on screen. If the refetch brings a newer version of a task while the user has unsaved edits to it, the detail screen says "Changed elsewhere" straight away and offers to review or reload. Second, the guarantee: each task has an integer version, sent as an ETag. PATCH with If-Match updates only if the version still matches (UPDATE … WHERE id = :id AND owner_id = :me AND version = :v), otherwise it returns 412. The detail screen always sends If-Match. PATCH changes only the fields sent.
279	Why both
280	Refreshing on focus prevents most mismatches but can't catch them all. It mustn't overwrite a half-typed draft, a change from another device can land while this tab keeps focus, and scripted clients have no focus at all. The version check catches everything else in one conditional UPDATE, with no locks.
281	 | Race | Guard | Test that proves it
282	 | Two sign-ups with one email | Unique index on email; the insert's IntegrityError becomes 409. Never check-then-insert. | Integration: 20 concurrent sign-ups, exactly one 201 and nineteen 409s
283	 | Moves and creates in one list at once | Per-user advisory lock, unique (owner_id, rank) | Integration: 50 concurrent moves; afterwards the ranks are unique and the list holds the same tasks. Live: the same through both replicas
284	 | Two tabs edit one task | Refetch on focus; "Changed elsewhere" notice; version, If-Match, 412 | Integration: two PATCHes on the same version, one 200 and one 412. Component: a newer version arriving under a draft shows the notice
285	 | Edit or toggle after delete | Owner-scoped UPDATE affects 0 rows → 404 | Component: a 404 on a mutation removes the row and says why
286	 | A late search response overwrites a newer one | Results cached per search term; superseded requests aborted with AbortSignal | Hook test: MSW delays the response for "ab" past the one for "abc", and "abc" stays on screen
287	 | A refetch lands on top of an optimistic reorder | cancelQueries before the optimistic write; reorder mutations share one scope, so they run in order | Component: three quick moves end in the order the user made
288	 | Something blocks the event loop | Async-only handlers, hashing off the loop (D13, D14) | Backend fixture: asyncio debug mode with a 50 ms slow-callback threshold; a test fails if any callback blocks longer
289	 | Load beyond the limits | Request, connection and hash limits; 503 with the envelope (D13 to D15) | Load test (D18): no 5xx at target load, p95 within budget
290	D18
291	### A load test before submissionlocked
292	Choice
293	k6, run from its official container as a compose profile (docker compose --profile load run k6), so nothing needs installing. 200 virtual users, each with its own account, ramp up over 1 minute and hold for 3. Each one loops: list, search, create, toggle, move, edit, delete, with 1 second of think time. After the run, a check script confirms every user's list has unique ranks and the expected number of tasks.
294	Pass
295	Under 0.1% failed requests and no 5xx. p95 latency under 250 ms for reads and under 400 ms for writes; under 1.5 s for sign-in, which queues on purpose (D14). Results are saved with the machine's specs and quoted in the README.
296	Instead of
297	Locust, which is Python and fits the backend, but lacks k6's built-in pass/fail thresholds.
298	Why
299	It shows the limits in D13 to D16 working under real concurrency, and gives reviewers a script they can rerun at their own scale.
300	Capacity
301	A second, stepped run raises the number of users until a budget breaks. The last step that passed is the round's capacity figure for the final report (D15). It's repeated in rounds 2 and 3.
302	Run with
303	The lead. Scripts and budgets are reviewed before the first run, and results are walked through together.
304	### How we explain it in the deep-dive
305	- One request, end to end: every log line carries request_id, user_id, duration_ms and the replica that served it, so a single slow or failed request can be followed across both replicas.
306	- Each race has a test with the race in its name, from the table above, and each one fails if its guard is removed.
307	- The load test summary (throughput, p95 per endpoint, error rate, the consistency check) goes in the README next to this section's diagrams.
308	    Contract
309	## Endpoints
310	Every write also returns 403 if its Origin doesn't match the app, and every task endpoint returns 401 without a valid session. Those two codes aren't repeated in each row below.
311	 | Method and path | Does | Success | Errors
312	 | POST /api/v1/auth/register | Create an account and sign in | 201 | 400, 409
313	 | POST /api/v1/auth/login | Sign in; sets the session cookie | 200 | 400, 401
314	 | POST /api/v1/auth/logout | Clear the session cookie | 204 | none
315	 | GET /api/v1/auth/me | Who is signed in | 200 | 401
316	 | GET /api/v1/tasks?q= | List own tasks in rank order, optionally searched | 200 | 400
317	 | POST /api/v1/tasks | Create a task at the top | 201 | 400
318	 | GET /api/v1/tasks/{id} | Read one task | 200 | 404
319	 | PATCH /api/v1/tasks/{id} | Change any of title, notes, completed, due date; honours If-Match | 200 | 400, 404, 412
320	 | PUT /api/v1/tasks/{id}/position | Move after another task, or to the top | 200 | 400, 404
321	 | DELETE /api/v1/tasks/{id} | Delete a task | 204 | 404
322	 | GET /api/docs · /api/openapi.json | Interactive API docs and the OpenAPI document, for scripting | 200 | none
323	 | GET /livez | Liveness: the process is up and its loop answers. Checks no dependencies. | 200 | none
324	 | GET /readyz | Readiness: SELECT 1 within 1 s, and not shutting down | 200 | 503
325	D19
326	### Health checks: /livez and /readyzlocked
327	Choice
328	Two probes at the API root, outside /api/v1. Nginx doesn't route them, so only Docker and Kubernetes reach them. Liveness checks nothing but the process. Readiness checks the database and starts failing as soon as shutdown begins.
329	Instead of
330	/health, or a single /healthz.
331	Why
332	No standard path exists: the IETF's health-check format never went past a draft. The trailing z is Google's convention for keeping probe paths clear of app routes. Kubernetes deprecated /healthz for its own API server in v1.16 in favour of separate /livez and /readyz, and we follow that split. Keeping them separate matters: if liveness checked the database, a short database outage would make Kubernetes restart every API pod at once, turning a blip into an outage. Readiness only takes a pod out of rotation.
333	List responses are wrapped as {"items": [...]}, so a paging cursor can be added later without breaking the client. An after_id that doesn't exist and one that belongs to someone else get the same 400, so the response doesn't reveal which it was.
334	    Schema
335	## Two tables
336	 | Table | Columns | Constraints and indexes
337	 | users | id uuid · email citext · password_hash text · created_at timestamptz | Primary key on id; email unique, compared case-insensitively
338	 | tasks | id uuid · owner_id uuid · title varchar(200) · notes text · completed bool · due_date date null · rank text collate "C" · version integer · created_at, updated_at timestamptz | owner_id references users, delete cascades; unique index (owner_id, rank); trigram GIN index on title and notes; checks on title and notes length
339	    Frontend
340	## Screens
341	 | Route | Screen | Notes
342	 | /sign-in | Landing: sign in | Link to sign-up. After sign-in, goes back to the page that asked for it.
343	 | /sign-up | Create account | Errors shown next to each field, checked by the same Zod schema the API layer uses.
344	 | /tasks | Task list | Search box, quick add at the top, a checkbox on each row, drag by mouse, touch or keyboard. Empty, loading and error states.
345	 | /tasks/:id | Task detail | View and edit every field, save, and delete with a confirm step built into the page. Shows "Changed elsewhere" when a newer version arrives under unsaved edits.
346	 | * | Not found | Also shown for a task id that isn't yours.
347	- Responsive: one column from 320 px wide, a centred reading width on desktop, and 44 px touch targets.
348	- Server data lives only in TanStack Query. Toggle, reorder and delete update the screen immediately, roll back on error and show what failed. Create and edit wait for the server and show progress.
349	- Expired session: a 401 on any request clears the cache and goes to sign-in with a return path, handled once in the query client.
350	    Each layer earns its place
351	## Tests
352	Each behaviour is tested once, at the lowest layer that can catch it. Red, then green, inside the session. Every commit is green.
353	 | Layer | Tool | Owns | Runs against
354	 | Backend unit | pytest, Hypothesis | Rank maths (property-based), search pattern escaping, patch application, token and password helpers | Nothing; pure functions
355	 | Backend integration | pytest, httpx ASGI transport, asyncio.TaskGroup | Every endpoint's success and error codes, response shapes, ownership, persistence, the 422-to-400 mapping, the concurrent races above, and that Postgres sorts ranks the same way Python does | A real Postgres (the compose db; a service container in CI)
356	 | Frontend unit and component | Vitest (Jest's API), React Testing Library, MSW | Helpers, hooks, and each screen's states, optimistic rollback, field errors | jsdom, with fetch mocked at the boundary
357	 | Live API | pytest, httpx | Migrations ran, the proxy and cookie path work, a session from one replica works on the other, deep links serve the SPA, security headers are set | The compose stack on :8080
358	 | Browser end to end | Playwright | Four journeys: sign up and sign in; create, edit, complete; reorder and search; delete and sign out. Plus one at phone size | The compose stack on :8080
359	 | Load | k6 (container) | Throughput, latency and error budgets with 200 concurrent users, and data consistency afterwards (D18) | The compose stack on :8080, before submission
360	    Sequence
361	## Order of work: design before frontend code
362	- You sign off this spec.
363	- In parallel: the detailed coding plan (docs/plans/round-1.md), and a design artifact showing the tokens and every screen in every state.
364	- Gate: you review the design tokens and the screens. Changes go into the tokens and components, and the artifact is republished.
365	- Gate: the walkthrough of the coding instructions, with code, comment-style and type-checking samples.
366	- PRs, each reviewed by you after the card: skeleton, spec and plan, backend API, frontend (connecting the reviewed screens to real data), then containers with the live, browser and load tests.
367	- Gate: round 1 is done (below), then round 2.
368	D20
369	### The design artifact is built from the real componentslocked
370	Choice
371	Tokens go in frontend/src/styles/tokens.css as Tailwind 4 @theme variables (colour, type, spacing, radius, motion, light and dark). Building blocks go in frontend/src/components/ui/. Each screen is a view that takes its data and callbacks as props and does no fetching. A second Vite entry, frontend/design/, renders the token sheet and every view in every state with sample data, at phone and desktop widths. It is built into one self-contained HTML file and published as the artifact. Later, the frontend PR wraps each view in a small container that connects it to TanStack Query.
372	Instead of
373	Drawing the screens in a separate design tool or artifact type, then building them again in React.
374	Why
375	Nothing is built twice: what you approve is the code that ships. Splitting views from containers also keeps the views pure functions of their props, which makes them easy to test and easy to explain.
376	Direction
377	From the lead: a stellar look, a premium feel, vintage colours, zero redundancy.
378	Flag
379	This puts the first frontend code before the instructions walkthrough. To keep that safe, it follows the coding standards from the first line, the views hold no data logic the walkthrough could change, component tests come in the same commits, and it stays on feature/web-design-system. Its PR waits until the walkthrough is done.
380	Waits outside our control: about 2 minutes of CI per push, plus your review of each PR and of the design.
381	    Why round 1 is shaped this way
382	## What changes in rounds 2 and 3
383	The images, the app code and the probes stay the same in all three rounds. Only what surrounds them changes, which is why round 1 already has one origin, a one-shot migration and two replicas.
384	 | Concern | Round 1 · compose | Round 2 · k3d | Round 3 · AKS
385	 | Front door | nginx in web | Traefik Ingress (built into k3d) | Managed ingress with TLS
386	 | API scale | 2 replicas | Deployment, 3 replicas, rolling updates | Same, plus a pod autoscaler
387	 | Database | Postgres container and volume | Postgres StatefulSet | Azure Database for PostgreSQL
388	 | Migrations | One-shot service | Job before rollout | Job, run by the workflow
389	 | Secrets | Env file the human creates | Kubernetes Secret the human creates | Key Vault through the CSI driver
390	 | Images | Built locally | Imported into k3d, tagged with the git sha | Azure Container Registry, pushed by GitHub Actions (OIDC sign-in, no stored keys)
391	 | Manifests | None | Kustomize base + k3d overlay | Same base + aks overlay
392	    Exit criteria
393	## Round 1 is done when
394	### It works
395	- On a clean Mac, docker compose up --build brings up the stack and localhost:8080 lets a new user sign up and use every feature.
396	- Two users never see each other's tasks, through the UI or the API.
397	- The layout holds at phone width and at desktop width.
398	### It's proven
399	- All five test layers are green and above the coverage floors; you've reviewed the code.
400	- The load test passes its budgets, every user's data checks out afterwards, and the round's capacity figure is recorded.
401	- CI runs hygiene, backend, frontend and end-to-end jobs once the GitHub remote exists.
402	- The README covers running round 1 on a Mac.
403	    Not in round 1
404	## Later, in FUTURE.md
405	- Sign-in with Microsoft, Google or Apple (OpenID Connect), chosen per client. Refresh-token rotation and revocation.
406	- AI task entry: describe a new task or a change in text or voice, and the app makes it. Only once everything else works.
407	- AI summary home page for the user's tasks, possibly built on the AG-UI protocol.
408	- Account care: email verification and password reset. Data care: a rank rebalancing job, and paging for long lists.
409	    Sign-off record
410	## Signed off
411	D1 to D20 are locked. Revision 1 settled D3, D4, D6, D7, D8, D10 and D12. Revision 2's D13 to D20 were signed off on 2026-10-19, with these notes from the lead:
412	- D15: report realistic concurrent-user numbers at the end of each round, measured by the stepped load test.
413	- D16 and D18: the lead takes part in the race tests and the load tests.
414	- D17: a tab refreshes when the user comes back to it. Kept as the first layer, with the version check as the guarantee.
415	- Design: a stellar look, a premium feel, vintage colours and zero redundancy.
416	The detailed coding plan (docs/plans/round-1.md) and the design artifact are now being written in parallel.
417	  Drafted by Claude (agent) for review by the project lead. Revision 1 reviewed and answered by the lead; revision 2 added D13 to D20; revision 3 records their sign-off. Decisions marked locked are recorded in docs/kickoff.md.

## One origin, two API replicas, one database
The browser only ever talks to web on port 8080. Nginx serves the built SPA and forwards /api/* to the API, so the app and the API share one origin: no CORS, and the session cookie stays first-party. Running two API replicas already in round 1 proves the backend keeps no state in memory, one round before Kubernetes depends on it.

D4
### Session: a signed token in an httpOnly cookielocked
Choice
On sign-in the API sets a JWT (HS256, 8-hour lifetime) as cookie session: HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict, Path=/api, Secure once TLS exists in rounds 2 and 3. Sign-out clears it. Any replica can verify it with the shared secret.
Instead of
A bearer token in localStorage, which any injected script can read. Or a sessions table, which can be revoked but adds a lookup per request.
Why
Stateless across replicas and out of reach of page scripts. CSRF is covered by SameSite=Strict, the single origin, JSON-only request bodies and an Origin check on every write.
Costs
A token can't be revoked before it expires. Refresh-token rotation with a deny list is the round 3 hardening item.
Later
Sign-in with Microsoft, Google or Apple (OpenID Connect), chosen per client. Recorded in FUTURE.md.

D6
### Ordering by fractional rankslocked
Choice
Each task has a rank string, and the list is sorted by rank. A move computes a new rank between its new neighbours, so it changes one row. New tasks go to the top. Reordering is turned off while a search is active, because moving within a filtered subset is ambiguous.
Instead of
Integer positions renumbered on every move, or gapped integers with occasional rebalancing.
Why
One write per move whatever the list size, no renumbering, and the rank maths is a pure function we can test with generated inputs (see the figure below).
Costs
Ranks get longer when many tasks are dropped into the same gap. In practice that's a character or so per move into one spot; a rebalancing job goes on the "more time" list.

Choice

Instead of
Filtering the loaded list in the browser.
Why
The API owns operations on the data, the index keeps search fast as lists grow, and paging can come later without changing how search behaves.

D9
### HTTP contractlocked
Choice
Resources under /api/v1. Success: 200, 201 with a Location header, 204. Errors: 400 for validation (FastAPI's 422 is remapped), 401 when the session is missing or bad, 403 when a write comes from another origin, 404 for a missing task or one owned by someone else, 409 when an email is already registered, 412 when an edit is based on an old version (D17), 503 when the API is overloaded or the database is unreachable (D13, D15). ## A move writes one row
Moving “Buy milk” from the bottom to just below “Call Sam”. With integer positions, every task between the old and new place is renumbered. With ranks, only the moved task gets a new key, halfway between its new neighbours. ## Async and concurrency
Each API replica is one uvicorn process running one event loop. The loop can hold thousands of open requests, but only while each of them is waiting on I/O. Anything that keeps the loop busy (a slow hash, a blocking call, a synchronous write) stalls every request on that replica at once. So the design has three jobs: never block the loop, put a limit on every shared resource, and when a limit is reached, make requests queue for a bounded time or get a clear 503 rather than pile up.

D13
### One uvicorn process per container, every handler asynclocked
Choice
uvicorn[standard] (uvloop, httptools) with one worker per container; more capacity means more replicas. Every route is async def and uses only async libraries. --limit-concurrency 200 answers 503 past 200 in-flight requests. --timeout-graceful-shutdown 20 lets in-flight requests finish on SIGTERM, then the lifespan closes the pool. Nginx keeps connections to the API open and caps request bodies at 64 KB.
Instead of
Gunicorn or uvicorn managing several worker processes inside one container. Or plain def handlers, which FastAPI runs on a thread pool capped at 40 threads by default.
Why
One process per container lets Docker and Kubernetes restart it, count it and scale it, and each pod's memory and CPU stay predictable. Async-only handlers mean the loop is the only scheduler to reason about.
D14
### Password hashing runs off the loop, at most four at a timelocked
Choice
argon2id with OWASP's parameters (19 MiB memory, 2 passes, 1 lane), run through asyncio.to_thread behind an asyncio.Semaphore(4) per process. argon2-cffi releases the GIL while it hashes, so the hashes really do run in parallel with the loop.
Instead of
Hashing on the loop, or without a limit.
Why
One hash takes tens of milliseconds of CPU. On the loop, every sign-in would freeze that replica for that long. Without a limit, a burst of sign-ins would exhaust memory: the library's default profile uses 64 MiB per hash, so 100 sign-ins at once would need over 6 GB. With the semaphore, extra sign-ins wait their turn instead.
D15
### A connection budget, and timeouts on every waitlocked
Choice
Async SQLAlchemy on asyncpg. Each replica has a pool of 10 connections plus 5 overflow, a 5-second wait for a free one, and pool_pre_ping. Postgres runs with statement_timeout 5 s and idle_in_transaction_session_timeout 10 s. Each request gets its own AsyncSession and one transaction, committed on success and rolled back on any exception. Sessions are never shared between concurrent coroutines, because an AsyncSession isn't safe for that.
Budget
Total connections = replicas × 15, kept under 80% of Postgres's 100. That's 30 in round 1 and 45 in round 2. Round 3 adds autoscaling, so it puts the PgBouncer built into Azure's Postgres in front.
Why
Requests are short, so 15 connections serve many concurrent users. When load exceeds that, requests wait up to 5 seconds and then get a clear 503, rather than an unbounded queue taking down the database.
Reported
The final report states, for each round, how many concurrent users the stack served within budget, measured by D18 rather than estimated.
    Many requests touching the same rows
## Races and consistency
Tasks are private, so two different users never contend for the same row. The races that remain come from one user (two tabs, fast drags, a double-click) and from users signing up with the same email. Every guard lives in Postgres, because a lock inside one Python process means nothing to the other replica.

          Postgres

          waits
          BEGIN · lock(owner) granted

          read neighbours a0 | a1

Both requests ask to place a task right after A. The shaded bars show who holds the per-user lock (pg_advisory_xact_lock on the owner id; it's released at commit). Without it, both would read a0 | a1 and both would write a0V. The unique index on (owner_id, rank) would then reject one, and the user would see an error instead of a silent tie. Other users' writes never wait for this lock.
D16
### Order changes are serialized per user, in Postgreslocked
Choice
Creating a task and moving one each start their transaction with pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtextextended(owner_id::text, 0)), then read the neighbours, compute the rank and write. A unique index on (owner_id, rank) backs it up. Edits and deletes don't take the lock, since they never change ranks.
Isolation
Postgres's default, READ COMMITTED, and that's deliberate. Each statement reads a fresh snapshot, so the neighbour read after the lock is granted sees the other move's commit. Under REPEATABLE READ the snapshot would be taken at the lock statement, before that commit, and both moves would compute the same rank.
Instead of
An asyncio.Lock, which only covers one process. SERIALIZABLE everywhere, which needs retry loops on every write. A version check on the whole list.
Why
The lock is the narrowest correct one: one user's ordering writes queue for a few milliseconds, and nothing else waits.
Testing
The race tests run with the lead present. We watch them fail with the lock removed, then pass with it in place, before the backend PR is raised.
D17
### Tabs stay fresh, and edits can't silently overwrite each otherlocked
The case
Tab 2 loaded a task before tab 1 saved a change to it. Tab 2 then saves its stale copy, and tab 1's change is silently lost.
Choice
Two layers. First, freshness: whenever a tab regains focus or the network comes back, TanStack Query refetches what's on screen. If the refetch brings a newer version of a task while the user has unsaved edits to it, the detail screen says "Changed elsewhere" straight away and offers to review or reload. Second, the guarantee: each task has an integer version, sent as an ETag. PATCH with If-Match updates only if the version still matches (UPDATE … WHERE id = :id AND owner_id = :me AND version = :v), otherwise it returns 412. The detail screen always sends If-Match. PATCH changes only the fields sent.
Why both
Refreshing on focus prevents most mismatches but can't catch them all. It mustn't overwrite a half-typed draft, a change from another device can land while this tab keeps focus, and scripted clients have no focus at all. The version check catches everything else in one conditional UPDATE, with no locks.

### A load test before submissionlocked
Choice
k6, run from its official container as a compose profile (docker compose --profile load run k6), so nothing needs installing. 200 virtual users, each with its own account, ramp up over 1 minute and hold for 3. The lead. Scripts and budgets are reviewed before the first run, and results are walked through together.

D19
### Health checks: /livez and /readyzlocked
Choice
Two probes at the API root, outside /api/v1. Nginx doesn't route them, so only Docker and Kubernetes reach them. Liveness checks nothing but the process. Readiness checks the database and starts failing as soon as shutdown begins.
Instead of
/health, or a single /healthz.
Why
No standard path exists: the IETF's health-check format never went past a draft. The trailing z is Google's convention for keeping probe paths clear of app routes. Kubernetes deprecated /healthz for its own API server in v1.16 in favour of separate /livez and /readyz, and we follow that split. Keeping them separate matters: if liveness checked the database, a short database outage would make Kubernetes restart every API pod at once, turning a blip into an outage. Readiness only takes a pod out of rotation.
List responses are wrapped as {"items": [...]}, so a paging cursor can be added later without breaking the client. An after_id that doesn't exist and one that belongs to someone else get the same 400, so the response doesn't reveal which it was.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Fail when shipped code carries task markers, debugger hooks, focused tests or debug-only logging."""

import re
import subprocess
import sys
from collections.abc import Callable, Iterable, Iterator
from dataclasses import dataclass
from pathlib import Path, PurePosixPath

PathFilter = Callable[[PurePosixPath], bool]

ROOTS = ("backend", "frontend", "e2e", "deploy")
TEXT_SUFFIXES = frozenset(
    {
        ".py",
        ".ts",
        ".tsx",
        ".js",
        ".jsx",
        ".mjs",
        ".css",
        ".html",
        ".yml",
        ".yaml",
        ".toml",
        ".cfg",
        ".ini",
        ".sh",
    }
)
SKIP_PARTS = frozenset(
    {
        "node_modules",
        ".venv",
        "dist",
        "build",
        "coverage",
        "playwright-report",
        "test-results",
    }
)


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Check:
    """One forbidden pattern and the files it applies to."""

    label: str
    pattern: re.Pattern[str]
    applies: PathFilter


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Hit:
    """One line that failed a check."""

    label: str
    path: PurePosixPath
    line_no: int
    line: str


def suffix_in(*suffixes: str) -> PathFilter:
    """Build a filter that accepts paths with one of the given suffixes."""
    return lambda path: path.suffix in suffixes


def under(prefix: str) -> PathFilter:
    """Build a filter that accepts paths below the given folder."""
    return lambda path: path.is_relative_to(prefix)


def all_of(*filters: PathFilter) -> PathFilter:
    """Combine filters so a path must pass every one."""
    return lambda path: all(f(path) for f in filters)


def negate(f: PathFilter) -> PathFilter:
    """Invert a filter."""
    return lambda path: not f(path)


is_python = suffix_in(".py")
is_script = suffix_in(".ts", ".tsx", ".js", ".jsx", ".mjs")


def is_test(path: PurePosixPath) -> bool:
    """True for backend tests and frontend `*.test.*` or `*.spec.*` files."""
    return (
        under("backend/tests")(path) or ".test." in path.name or ".spec." in path.name
    )


CHECKS = (
    Check("task marker", re.compile(r"\b(TODO|FIXME|XXX|HACK)\b"), lambda _: True),
    Check("python debugger", re.compile(r"\bbreakpoint\(|\bpdb\b"), is_python),
    Check(
        "print in backend code (use logging)",
        re.compile(r"^\s*print\("),
        all_of(is_python, negate(is_test)),
    ),
    Check("javascript debugger", re.compile(r"\bdebugger\b"), is_script),
    Check(
        "debug-only console call (use console.info, warn or error)",
        re.compile(r"\bconsole\.(log|debug|trace)\("),
        is_script,
    ),
    Check(
        "focused test",
        re.compile(r"\b(it|test|describe)\.only\("),
        all_of(is_script, is_test),
    ),
)


def repo_root() -> Path:
    """Return the top of the git work tree."""
    out = subprocess.run(
        ["git", "rev-parse", "--show-toplevel"],
        capture_output=True,
        text=True,
        check=True,
    ).stdout
    return Path(out.strip())


def candidate_files(root: Path) -> list[PurePosixPath]:
    """List tracked and untracked, non-ignored text files under the code roots."""
    out = subprocess.run(
        ["git", "ls-files", "--cached", "--others", "--exclude-standard", "--", *ROOTS],
        cwd=root,
        capture_output=True,
        text=True,
        check=True,
    ).stdout
    paths = (PurePosixPath(line) for line in out.splitlines())
    return sorted(
        {
            p
            for p in paths
            if p.suffix in TEXT_SUFFIXES and SKIP_PARTS.isdisjoint(p.parts)
        }
    )


def scan(root: Path, path: PurePosixPath, checks: Iterable[Check]) -> Iterator[Hit]:
    """Yield every line in one file that fails a check that applies to it."""
    applicable = tuple(c for c in checks if c.applies(path))
    if not applicable:
        return
    try:
        lines = (root / path).read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines()
    except (OSError, UnicodeDecodeError):
        return
    yield from (
        Hit(c.label, path, n, line.strip())
        for n, line in enumerate(lines, start=1)
        for c in applicable
        if c.pattern.search(line)
    )


def main() -> int:
    """Scan the repo and print each hit; return 1 when there is any."""
    root = repo_root()
    hits = [hit for path in candidate_files(root) for hit in scan(root, path, CHECKS)]
    for hit in hits:
        print(f"{hit.path}:{hit.line_no}: {hit.label}: {hit.line}")
    print(
        f"hygiene check {'failed' if hits else 'passed'}: {len(hits)} finding(s)",
        file=sys.stderr if hits else sys.stdout,
    )
    return 1 if hits else 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

---
name: claude-docs-check
description: Check whether the branch's changes need updates to CLAUDE.md, the rules or the skills, and make them on Opus. Runs before every PR to the base branch.
---
# Claude docs check

1. Base branch is `main` unless told otherwise. Changed files: `git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD`.
2. Match them against `map.json` in this folder. Each entry maps code paths to the instruction files that describe them. No match: say "no docs triggers on this branch" and stop; the PR hook will not block.
3. On a match, run the `docs-keeper` agent with the base branch, the changed files and the matched entries. It runs on Opus and either edits the mapped files or explains, per artifact, why nothing needs to change.
4. Read its edits back against the code, not against the commit messages. Fix anything wrong.
5. Commit its decision. With edits: commit the docs files with the trailer `Claude-Docs: updated (<files>)`. Without edits: an empty commit whose message is `chore(claude): docs check, no change needed` with the trailer `Claude-Docs: no change: <reason>`. The PR hook reads that trailer.
6. Report what changed and why, in one paragraph.
=========== .claude/skills/raise-pr/SKILL.md
---
name: raise-pr
description: Show the pre-raise card for a pull request and open it only after the human says yes.
disable-model-invocation: true
---
# Raise a PR

Do these steps in order. Stop after step 4 and wait.

1. Sync: `git fetch --all --prune`, then report behind/ahead against the base branch. Rebase if behind. With no remote yet, say so and skip.
2. Check the branch: every commit is on a branch off `main`, the tree is clean, and `/verify` has passed. Run `/claude-docs-check`; the PR hook blocks `gh pr create` until its decision is on the branch.
3. Build the card:
   - Title: `type(scope): subject`. Types: feat, fix, chore, docs, refactor, perf, test, ci, build, revert, release. Subject starts lowercase, no trailing period.
   - Branch and base (usually `main`).
   - Assignee: the GitHub login of the human whose git identity is on the commits. `git log -1 --format=%an` gives the name; `gh api user --jq .login` confirms the login.
   - Label: one, from the branch prefix through `CONTRIBUTING.md` § 2. If the label does not exist on the repo yet (`gh label list`), say so on the card; creating it is part of the yes.
   - Summary: one to three lines. The problem and the chosen approach.
   - Description with the sections What, Why, How to test, Risks and rollback. Link sources rather than restating them. End with the attribution footer the session gives you.
4. Show the card and the description in chat. Ask for a go. Do not push or create anything yet.
5. On a yes: create the label if the card said it was missing, `git push -u origin <branch>`, then `gh pr create --base <base> --head <branch> --title "<title>" --body-file <file> --assignee <login> --label <label>`. The commands prompt for permission; that is expected.
6. Report the PR URL, then `gh pr checks <n> --watch` and report the result.

Never add reviewers unless the human names them. Never open a second PR for the same branch.
=========== .claude/skills/repo-sync/SKILL.md
---
name: repo-sync
description: Sync this repo (and any sibling repos it is coupled to) to the latest base branch at the start of a session, and report state.
---
# Repo sync

Run this before writing code and before raising a PR.

1. This repo: `git fetch --all --prune --tags`, then `git rev-list --left-right --count origin/main...HEAD`. Left is behind, right is ahead. Behind above zero on a feature branch means rebase first. Report the numbers; "already current" is information too.
2. Siblings, if this repo shares a contract with others: for each sibling (`../<repo>`, base `<branch>`), fetch, then report current branch, dirty count, behind/ahead of its base. If a sibling is pinned by a ref file here, confirm the sibling's checkout matches the pin before trusting a local test run. No siblings: say so and skip this step.
3. A clean sibling that is only behind may be fast-forwarded. Never switch a sibling's branch without saying so, and put it back afterwards. Never pull or stash a dirty sibling; report it and let the human decide.
4. If `.git/index.lock` exists and no git process is running, it is a stale lock from a crashed process. Say so, then remove it.

Report one line per repo: branch, head, behind/ahead, dirty count.
=========== .claude/skills/verify/SKILL.md
---
name: verify
description: Run the checks that make "done" true before reporting a task complete or committing. No side effects beyond running checks and tests.
---
# Verify before saying done

1. Gates. Run what CI runs for every part the change touched, from the repo root. Skip a part only when it does not exist yet, and say so.
   - Hygiene: `python3 scripts/check_hygiene.py`
   - Hooks, when `.claude/hooks/` changed: `python3 -m unittest discover -s .claude/hooks/tests`
   - Backend: `cd backend && uv run ruff check . && uv run ruff format --check . && uv run mypy && uv run pytest`
   - Frontend: `cd frontend && npm run check && npm run test && npm run build`
   - When the change touches the running stack (Dockerfiles, compose, manifests, config, CORS, routing): bring the stack up and run the live-server e2e and Playwright suites against it, following `CONTRIBUTING.md` § 14 for restarts.
   Report the exact counts per suite and the stack each ran against. A failure is reported as a failure, with the output.
2. Read back. Read `git diff` for every file you changed. Check each hunk does what the task asked and nothing more.
3. Logs. For every log line in the diff, say what it helps someone monitor. Delete any line added only to debug.
4. Tests. For every test in the diff, name the failure it catches that no other test catches. Delete a test that has none.
5. Side effects. For every function, component, model, field or constant you changed or removed, grep the repo for other users. Fix or list them.
6. Secrets. Scan the diff for keys, tokens, passwords, connection strings. None may be in it.
7. Contract check, when the change sends data across a boundary: read the receiving side's type first (the Pydantic model, the Zod schema, the migration), not the docs, and convert explicitly. A change to an API model changes the Zod schema in the same PR.
8. Plan adherence, when working from a written plan: diff your output against the plan's fields, endpoints and names. Anything missing or extra is a bug until the human says otherwise.

Then report: what was verified, what was not, and why.

=========== .claude/agents/reviewer.md
---
name: reviewer
description: Adversarial reviewer for a branch or PR. Use before a human reads the diff. Finds correctness bugs, scope creep, missing or redundant tests and rule violations, then writes up the assumptions the author made.
model: opus
memory: project
tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash
---
You review code written by another agent or a person. You have not seen their conversation, so you do not share their blind spots. Be specific and be fair.

Input: a branch name or a PR number. Start with `git diff origin/main...<branch>` or `gh pr diff <n>`.

Cover all of:
1. Correctness. Does each hunk do what the commit message says? Trace inputs to outputs for anything that crosses a boundary, and read the receiving side's types. For the API: the status code for every error path matches `api-contract.md`, and every task query filters on the owner.
2. Scope. Anything in the diff the task did not ask for? Name it.
3. Tests. New behaviour without a test, a test that cannot fail, and a test that repeats what another layer already proves (`testing.md`, "Each layer earns its place"). Check that each commit is green on its own.
4. Style. Functional core and imperative shell: pure domain logic, no mutated inputs, `map`/`filter`/`reduce` and comprehensions over accumulator loops, composition over long functions, the right data structure for the access pattern. Async through the high-level abstraction (async SQLAlchemy, `TaskGroup`, TanStack Query), never `useEffect` plus `fetch`.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Fail when shipped code carries task markers, debugger hooks, focused tests or debug-only logging."""

import re
import subprocess
import sys
from collections.abc import Callable, Iterable, Iterator
from dataclasses import dataclass
from pathlib import Path, PurePosixPath

PathFilter = Callable[[PurePosixPath], bool]

ROOTS = ("backend", "frontend", "e2e", "deploy")
TEXT_SUFFIXES = frozenset(
    {
        ".py",
        ".ts",
        ".tsx",
        ".js",
        ".jsx",
        ".mjs",
        ".css",
        ".html",
        ".yml",
        ".yaml",
        ".toml",
        ".cfg",
        ".ini",
        ".sh",
    }
)
SKIP_PARTS = frozenset(
    {
        "node_modules",
        ".venv",
        "dist",
        "build",
        "coverage",
        "playwright-report",
        "test-results",
    }
)


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Check:
    """One forbidden pattern and the files it applies to."""

    label: str
    pattern: re.Pattern[str]
    applies: PathFilter


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Hit:
    """One line that failed a check."""

    label: str
    path: PurePosixPath
    line_no: int
    line: str


def suffix_in(*suffixes: str) -> PathFilter:
    """Build a filter that accepts paths with one of the given suffixes."""
    return lambda path: path.suffix in suffixes


def under(prefix: str) -> PathFilter:
    """Build a filter that accepts paths below the given folder."""
    return lambda path: path.is_relative_to(prefix)


def all_of(*filters: PathFilter) -> PathFilter:
    """Combine filters so a path must pass every one."""
    return lambda path: all(f(path) for f in filters)


def negate(f: PathFilter) -> PathFilter:
    """Invert a filter."""
    return lambda path: not f(path)


is_python = suffix_in(".py")
is_script = suffix_in(".ts", ".tsx", ".js", ".jsx", ".mjs")


def is_test(path: PurePosixPath) -> bool:
    """True for backend tests and frontend `*.test.*` or `*.spec.*` files."""
    return (
        under("backend/tests")(path) or ".test." in path.name or ".spec." in path.name
    )


CHECKS = (
    Check("task marker", re.compile(r"\b(TODO|FIXME|XXX|HACK)\b"), lambda _: True),
    Check("python debugger", re.compile(r"\bbreakpoint\(|\bpdb\b"), is_python),
    Check(
        "print in backend code (use logging)",
        re.compile(r"^\s*print\("),
        all_of(is_python, negate(is_test)),
    ),
    Check("javascript debugger", re.compile(r"\bdebugger\b"), is_script),
    Check(
        "debug-only console call (use console.info, warn or error)",
        re.compile(r"\bconsole\.(log|debug|trace)\("),
        is_script,
    ),
    Check(
        "focused test",
        re.compile(r"\b(it|test|describe)\.only\("),
        all_of(is_script, is_test),
    ),
)


def repo_root() -> Path:
    """Return the top of the git work tree."""
    out = subprocess.run(
        ["git", "rev-parse", "--show-toplevel"],
        capture_output=True,
        text=True,
        check=True,
    ).stdout
    return Path(out.strip())


def candidate_files(root: Path) -> list[PurePosixPath]:
    """List tracked and untracked, non-ignored text files under the code roots."""
    out = subprocess.run(
        ["git", "ls-files", "--cached", "--others", "--exclude-standard", "--", *ROOTS],
        cwd=root,
        capture_output=True,
        text=True,
        check=True,
    ).stdout
    paths = (PurePosixPath(line) for line in out.splitlines())
    return sorted(
        {
            p
            for p in paths
            if p.suffix in TEXT_SUFFIXES and SKIP_PARTS.isdisjoint(p.parts)
        }
    )


def scan(root: Path, path: PurePosixPath, checks: Iterable[Check]) -> Iterator[Hit]:
    """Yield every line in one file that fails a check that applies to it."""
    applicable = tuple(c for c in checks if c.applies(path))
    if not applicable:
        return
    try:
        lines = (root / path).read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines()
    except (OSError, UnicodeDecodeError):
        return
    yield from (
        Hit(c.label, path, n, line.strip())
        for n, line in enumerate(lines, start=1)
        for c in applicable
        if c.pattern.search(line)
    )


def main() -> int:
    """Scan the repo and print each hit; return 1 when there is any."""
    root = repo_root()
    hits = [hit for path in candidate_files(root) for hit in scan(root, path, CHECKS)]
    for hit in hits:
        print(f"{hit.path}:{hit.line_no}: {hit.label}: {hit.line}")
    print(
        f"hygiene check {'failed' if hits else 'passed'}: {len(hits)} finding(s)",
        file=sys.stderr if hits else sys.stdout,
    )
    return 1 if hits else 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

# Claude docs check

1. Base branch is `main` unless told otherwise. Changed files: `git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD`.
2. Match them against `map.json` in this folder. Each entry maps code paths to the instruction files that describe them. No match: say "no docs triggers on this branch" and stop; the PR hook will not block.
3. On a match, run the `docs-keeper` agent with the base branch, the changed files and the matched entries. It runs on Opus and either edits the mapped files or explains, per artifact, why nothing needs to change.
4. Read its edits back against the code, not against the commit messages. Fix anything wrong.
5. Commit its decision. With edits: commit the docs files with the trailer `Claude-Docs: updated (<files>)`. Without edits: an empty commit whose message is `chore(claude): docs check, no change needed` with the trailer `Claude-Docs: no change: <reason>`. The PR hook reads that trailer.
6. Report what changed and why, in one paragraph.

# Raise a PR

Do these steps in order. Stop after step 4 and wait.

1. Sync: `git fetch --all --prune`, then report behind/ahead against the base branch. Rebase if behind. With no remote yet, say so and skip.
2. Check the branch: every commit is on a branch off `main`, the tree is clean, and `/verify` has passed. Run `/claude-docs-check`; the PR hook blocks `gh pr create` until its decision is on the branch.
3. Build the card:
   - Title: `type(scope): subject`. Types: feat, fix, chore, docs, refactor, perf, test, ci, build, revert, release. Subject starts lowercase, no trailing period.
   - Branch and base (usually `main`).
   - Assignee: the GitHub login of the human whose git identity is on the commits. `git log -1 --format=%an` gives the name; `gh api user --jq .login` confirms the login.
   - Label: one, from the branch prefix through `CONTRIBUTING.md` § 2. If the label does not exist on the repo yet (`gh label list`), say so on the card; creating it is part of the yes.
   - Summary: one to three lines. The problem and the chosen approach.
   - Description with the sections What, Why, How to test, Risks and rollback. Link sources rather than restating them. End with the attribution footer the session gives you.
4. Show the card and the description in chat. Ask for a go. Do not push or create anything yet.
5. On a yes: create the label if the card said it was missing, `git push -u origin <branch>`, then `gh pr create --base <base> --head <branch> --title "<title>" --body-file <file> --assignee <login> --label <label>`. The commands prompt for permission; that is expected.
6. Report the PR URL, then `gh pr checks <n> --watch` and report the result.

Never add reviewers unless the human names them. Never open a second PR for the same branch.

# Repo sync

Run this before writing code and before raising a PR.

1. This repo: `git fetch --all --prune --tags`, then `git rev-list --left-right --count origin/main...HEAD`. Left is behind, right is ahead. Behind above zero on a feature branch means rebase first. Report the numbers; "already current" is information too.
2. Siblings, if this repo shares a contract with others: for each sibling (`../<repo>`, base `<branch>`), fetch, then report current branch, dirty count, behind/ahead of its base. If a sibling is pinned by a ref file here, confirm the sibling's checkout matches the pin before trusting a local test run. No siblings: say so and skip this step.
3. A clean sibling that is only behind may be fast-forwarded. Never switch a sibling's branch without saying so, and put it back afterwards. Never pull or stash a dirty sibling; report it and let the human decide.
4. If `.git/index.lock` exists and no git process is running, it is a stale lock from a crashed process. Say so, then remove it.

Report one line per repo: branch, head, behind/ahead, dirty count.

# Verify before saying done

1. Gates. Run what CI runs for every part the change touched, from the repo root. Skip a part only when it does not exist yet, and say so.
   - Hygiene: `python3 scripts/check_hygiene.py`
   - Hooks, when `.claude/hooks/` changed: `python3 -m unittest discover -s .claude/hooks/tests`
   - Backend: `cd backend && uv run ruff check . && uv run ruff format --check . && uv run mypy && uv run pytest`
   - Frontend: `cd frontend && npm run check && npm run test && npm run build`
   - When the change touches the running stack (Dockerfiles, compose, manifests, config, CORS, routing): bring the stack up and run the live-server e2e and Playwright suites against it, following `CONTRIBUTING.md` § 14 for restarts.
   Report the exact counts per suite and the stack each ran against. A failure is reported as a failure, with the output.
2. Read back. Read `git diff` for every file you changed. Check each hunk does what the task asked and nothing more.
3. Logs. For every log line in the diff, say what it helps someone monitor. Delete any line added only to debug.
4. Tests. For every test in the diff, name the failure it catches that no other test catches. Delete a test that has none.
5. Side effects. For every function, component, model, field or constant you changed or removed, grep the repo for other users. Fix or list them.
6. Secrets. Scan the diff for keys, tokens, passwords, connection strings. None may be in it.
7. Contract check, when the change sends data across a boundary: read the receiving side's type first (the Pydantic model, the Zod schema, the migration), not the docs, and convert explicitly. A change to an API model changes the Zod schema in the same PR.
8. Plan adherence, when working from a written plan: diff your output against the plan's fields, endpoints and names. Anything missing or extra is a bug until the human says otherwise.

Then report: what was verified, what was not, and why.

entries.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead. claude.ai artifact links (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}) are published artifacts: read them with the Artifact tool (action "read"), not WebFetch or curl.
- Fails on localhost and other hostnames without a dot; for a local server, use curl via Bash.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.

content.content:
**Short answer:** By default, the exit code runs **after** the response is sent. Setting `scope="function"` moves it to run **before** the response is sent. The page doesn't say anything explicit about exceptions raised inside the exit code itself, and it gives no version numbers.

## Timing

From the page:

> Normally the exit code of dependencies with `yield` is executed **after the response** is sent to the client.

> But if you know that you won't need to use the dependency after returning from the _path operation function_, you can use `Depends(scope="function")` to tell FastAPI that it should close the dependency after the _path operation function_ returns, but **before** the **response is sent**.

> Only the code prior to and including the `yield` statement is executed before creating a response

> The code following the `yield` statement is executed after the response

## The `scope` parameter

Yes, `Depends()` accepts `scope`, with two values:

> * `"function"`: start the dependency before the _path operation function_ that handles the request, end the dependency after the _path operation function_ ends, but **before** the response is sent back to the client.
> * `"request"`: start the dependency before the _path operation function_ that handles the request (similar to when using `"function"`), but end **after** the response is sent back to the client.

> If not specified and the dependency has `yield`, it will have a `scope` of `"request"` by default.

Example from the page:

```python
from typing import Annotated
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI

app = FastAPI()

def get_username():
    try:
        yield "Rick"
    finally:
        print("Cleanup up before response is sent")

@app.get("/users/me")
def get_user_me(username: Annotated[str, Depends(get_username, scope="function")]):
    return username
```

A sub-dependency rule also applies: when a dependency has `scope="request"` (the default), its sub-dependencies also need `scope="request"`. A `"function"`-scoped dependency can depend on both kinds.

## Exceptions

The page's exception guidance is about exceptions that occur during request handling, not about exceptions raised in the exit code:

> If you use a `try` block in a dependency with `yield`, you'll receive any exception that was thrown when using the dependency.

> If you catch an exception in a dependency with `yield`, unless you are raising another `HTTPException` or similar, **you should re-raise the original exception**.

> Now the client will get the same _HTTP 500 Internal Server Error_ response, but the server will have our custom `InternalError` in the logs.

The page also says that once a response has been sent, it can't be changed. The sequence diagram labels the point after the path operation returns as "Response is already sent, can't change it anymore," and notes that "Only **one response** will be sent to the client."

The page does not describe what happens if the exit code itself raises an exception.

## Version notes

This page has no version-specific notes. It only points to the advanced guide, [Advanced Dependencies - Dependencies with `yield`, `HTTPException`, `except` and Background Tasks](../../../advanced/advanced-dependencies/#dependencies-with-yield-httpexception-except-and-background-tasks), for how the behavior has changed across FastAPI versions. The page also doesn't state which version introduced `scope`.

content.content:
**Mutation scopes**

- The page says: "Per default, all mutations run in parallel - even if you invoke `.mutate()` of the same mutation multiple times." (Without a scope, mutations run concurrently.)
- Setting `scope.id` serializes mutations. "All mutations with the same `scope.id` will run in serial" (quoted, 58 characters).
- Mutations that arrive while another with the same scope is in progress start paused and wait in a queue. They resume automatically when their turn comes.
- Example: `useMutation({ mutationFn: addTodo, scope: { id: 'todo' } })`

**Version notes**

- The page has no version note for scopes.
- The only version reference is unrelated to scopes. It warns that calling `mutate` directly in an event callback won't work in React 16 and earlier, because of React event pooling.

**onMutate return value and rollback**

- `onMutate` runs before the mutation starts. Its return value is passed to the other callbacks as `onMutateResult`.
- The page's example returns `{ id: 1 }`, and the comment says the return value can be used for "rolling back." (Quoted fragment: "when for example rolling back".)
- In `onError`, the example logs a message about rolling back an optimistic update using `onMutateResult.id`.
- The callbacks receive a `context` argument, but the page doesn't define it. In the persistence example, `context.client` is used to call `cancelQueries`, `setQueryData`, and similar methods.
- The persistence example also shows a full optimistic-update pattern. `onMutate` adds an optimistic todo and returns it, `onSuccess` replaces it with the server result, and `onError` removes it.

content.content:
The page covers these topics, but it doesn't say what happens if exit code raises after the response has been sent.

## Version history

**Warning (quoted from the page):**
> You most probably don't need these technical details. These details are useful mainly if you had a FastAPI application older than 0.121.0 and you are facing issues with dependencies with `yield`.

**Scope and `Depends(scope=...)` (0.121.0):**
> In version 0.121.0, FastAPI added support for `Depends(scope="function")` for dependencies with `yield`.
>
> Using `Depends(scope="function")`, the exit code after `yield` is executed right after the _path operation function_ is finished, before the response is sent back to the client.
>
> And when using `Depends(scope="request")` (the default), the exit code after `yield` is executed after the response is sent.

**`StreamingResponse` (0.118.0):**
> Before FastAPI 0.118.0, if you used a dependency with `yield`, it would run the exit code after the _path operation function_ returned but right before sending the response.
>
> This change also meant that if you returned a `StreamingResponse`, the exit code of the dependency with `yield` would have been already run.
>
> This behavior was reverted in 0.118.0, to make the exit code after `yield` be executed after the response is sent.

**Early exit use case:** The page gives an example where a `Session` is closed early in a dependency, using `session.close()`, so the connection is released before a slow `StreamingResponse` finishes:
```python
def get_user(user_id: int, session: Annotated[Session, Depends(get_session)]):
    user = session.get(User, user_id)
    if not user:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=403, detail="Not authorized")
    session.close()
```

**`except` handling (0.110.0):**
> Before FastAPI 0.110.0, if you used a dependency with `yield`, and then you captured an exception with `except` in that dependency, and you didn't raise the exception again, the exception would be automatically raised/forwarded to any exception handlers or the internal server error handler.
>
> This was changed in version 0.110.0 to fix unhandled memory consumption from forwarded exceptions without a handler (internal server errors), and to make it consistent with the behavior of regular Python code.

**Background tasks (0.106.0):**
> Before FastAPI 0.106.0, raising exceptions after `yield` was not possible, the exit code in dependencies with `yield` was executed _after_ the response was sent, so Exception Handlers would have already run.
>
> This was changed in FastAPI 0.106.0 with the intention to not hold resources while waiting for the response to travel through the network.

> If you used to rely on this behavior, now you should create the resources for background tasks inside the background task itself, and use internally only data that doesn't depend on the resources of dependencies with `yield`.

## HTTPException

The page has no dedicated HTTPException section. It appears only in the examples above, where `get_user` raises `HTTPException(status_code=403, ...)`.

## If exit code raises after the response is sent

The page doesn't cover this case. It only says that with the default `scope="request"`, the exit code runs after the response is sent, and that before 0.106.0 exit code ran after the response but exceptions could not be raised from it. For the exact behavior, check the "Dependencies with yield" tutorial page, which the page links to, or the FastAPI source and issues.

**--limit-concurrency:** "Maximum number of concurrent connections or tasks to allow, before issuing HTTP 503 responses."

**--timeout-keep-alive:** "Close Keep-Alive connections if no new data is received within this timeout (in seconds)." Default: 5.

**--timeout-graceful-shutdown:** "Maximum number of seconds to wait for graceful shutdown. After this timeout, the server will start terminating requests."

**--no-access-log / access_log:** The page documents only the CLI flag: "Disable access log only, without changing log level." It doesn't cover an `access_log` keyword argument.

**--loop:** "The uvloop implementation provides greater performance, but is not compatible with Windows or PyPy."

**--http:** "The httptools implementation provides greater performance, but is not compatible with PyPy."

**--proxy-headers:** "Enable/Disable X-Forwarded-Proto, X-Forwarded-For to populate remote address info." It "Defaults to enabled, but is restricted to only trusting connecting IPs in the `forwarded-allow-ips` configuration."

**--forwarded-allow-ips:** "Comma separated list of IP Addresses, IP Networks, or literals (e.g. UNIX Socket path) to trust with proxy headers." Otherwise, "`127.0.0.1` and `::1` are trusted."

content.content:
**When the query key changes or the query becomes unused or out of date:**

- If the `signal` is consumed, the query is aborted. The page says that when a query "becomes out-of-date or inactive, this `signal` will become aborted."
- Consuming the signal cancels the promise: "the Promise will be cancelled (e.g. aborting the fetch)." The page also says the query is cancelled and its state is reverted to what it was before.
- Without a consumed signal, the query is not cancelled. It keeps running, and its result is still cached once it resolves.
- The page does not explicitly address query key changes. The closest match is the "out-of-date or inactive" wording above.

**Limitations:**

- Cancellation does not work with Suspense hooks. The page names `useSuspenseQuery`, `useSuspenseQueries`, and `useSuspenseInfiniteQuery`.

entries.name: SendMessage
entries.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will receive your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). A successful send means the message reached that session, not that its Claude read it: a session running in a different permission mode than yours holds cross-session messages for its user's approval (and may let them expire), and a session can refuse them outright — for a session on this machine a `[Cross-session delivery notice]` tells you when that happens (the tool result says when this session has no inbox for one to reach); for a Remote Control, cloud or Claude Desktop session nothing reports back, so never treat silence as agreement. Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you. The receiver reads your message literally in every case (idle or busy, on this machine, over Remote Control or headless): an `@` followed by a file path, or `@server:resource`, attaches nothing there, unlike in your own user's input. So never rely on `@` to deliver content: send the text itself, or a file with its own tool.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

## Protocol responses (legacy)

If you receive a JSON message with `type: "shutdown_request"` or `type: "plan_approval_request"`, respond with the matching `_response` type — echo the `request_id`, set `approve` true/false:

```json
{"to": "team-lead", "message": {"type": "shutdown_response", "request_id": "...", "approve": true}}
{"to": "researcher", "message": {"type": "plan_approval_response", "request_id": "...", "approve": false, "feedback": "add error handling"}}
```

Approving shutdown terminates your process. Rejecting plan sends the teammate back to revise. Don't originate `shutdown_request` unless asked. Don't send structured JSON status messages — report progress through your task tools if you have them, otherwise in plain prose.

to.description: Recipient: a name from ListAgents (append its " [ref]" only when a listing or an error shows one), a teammate name, "main", or a background agent's agentId

summary.description: A 5-10 word label for your own transcript row (not transmitted — the recipient previews the first line of `message`). Truncated to 200 characters rather than rejected.

anyOf.description: Plain text message content. The recipient's human sees only the FIRST LINE as a one-line preview until they expand it, so make the first line a clear, self-contained sentence saying what this is about — not a greeting, preamble, or bare @-mention.

notify_when_idle.description: Ask a session ON THIS MACHINE to send you ONE notice when it next goes idle (finishes its turn with nothing queued) or exits — opt-in, one-shot, no polling. With a message: deliver it now AND subscribe. Without a message (omit it): a pure subscription that costs the other session nothing.

input.summary: Send designer CSP and contract constraints
input.message:
Planner here: four constraints from the round 1 coding plan that touch your branch (nothing to reply unless one is a problem).
1. CSP. nginx will serve the SPA with `default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self'; font-src 'self'; img-src 'self' data:`. So fonts must be bundled (for example @fontsource packages or files under src/), not loaded from Google Fonts or another CDN, and no inline <style> or <script> in index.html. React `style={}` props are fine, because they go through the CSSOM.
2. Zod. `taskSchema` title should be `z.string().trim().min(1).max(200)` and notes `max(5000)`, to match the API, which strips the title. `dueDate` is `"YYYY-MM-DD"` or null. `credentialsSchema` is email (max 254) plus password 12 to 128 characters, used for both sign-in and sign-up.
3. Reorder contract. `TaskListView` should report a move as `onMove(taskId, afterId | null)`, where null means "to the top". The API takes `PUT /tasks/{id}/position {"afterId": ...}`, and the containers pass that straight through.
4. No crash or route-error view is in the agreed list (sign-in, sign-up, task-list, task-detail, not-found). The router's error boundary needs one. I'm listing it as an open question for the lead. If adding a small `ErrorView` (message and a retry or home action) is cheap for you, it would close the question.
